text: Every line an AI agent writes stands on someone else's work.
Eight levels down, a package most people have never heard of.
This is how infrastructure breaks. Quietly, then all at once.
And now, AI writes the code. Fewer people ever visit the docs, or the sponsor button.
But an AI agent is the first user of open source that knows exactly who it owes.
Nebraska pays the maintainers behind your coding agent's dependencies. Every month, by actual usage, through PayPal.
One click redirects to PayPal to approve a monthly budget. That is the agent's mandate, and its ceiling.
Then, one hook line. Only package names and depth leave the machine. Never source code.
At month end, the AI Treasurer answers typed questions about each package. How critical is it? How much do its maintainers need?
Same budget. The AI's judgment moves this package from sixty-nine dollars to a hundred and sixty-one.
A security advisory? The AI can propose a grant. Only a human can approve it, on PayPal.
A poisoned README tells the model to max out its score. The answer is rejected. Neutral weight.
A recipient changed their payout email yesterday. Held for review.
Then seven rules, enforced in code, before a single cent moves.
The AI decides where the money goes. The code decides where it can never go.
Maya, a fictional maintainer, sees exactly why she was paid. One sixty-one twenty-nine, plus the two-fifty grant.
Run it twice. One batch. No double pay.
Both sides get a statement anyone can recompute.
You can still choose not to pay. You just can't say you didn't know.
